This course follows a simulated study. The study starts with [genotypes](../docs/glossary.md#genotype). A genotype is the pair of DNA letters a person carries at one chosen position. The course ends with [association](../docs/glossary.md#association) results. An association is a statistical link between a DNA difference and a trait.

All data come from a computer program. They describe no real person. You do not need any programming experience.

Work in the same way at every step. Read the step. Follow the installation instructions in steps 0.1 to 0.4. From step 0.5, run each R command in the [console](../docs/glossary.md#console) of [RStudio](../docs/glossary.md#rstudio). Compare your result with the expected result. Then go to the next step.

Keep your computer's language and decimal settings as they are.

Validation: the R commands in this module ran without errors on Windows. The software installers and the password prompt in RStudio are checked by hand.

This [notebook](../docs/glossary.md#notebook) is the source of the guided preparation module. A notebook is a file that mixes text and R commands. The older file `01_quality_control.Rmd` is a separate, smaller demonstration.

Lesson text, figures and simulated data: [CC BY-NC-SA 4.0](../LICENSE-CONTENT.md). Code: [MIT](../LICENSE).

```{r knit_setup, include=FALSE}
start_dir <- setwd(if (file.exists("config.R")) "." else "..")
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = getwd())
setwd(start_dir)
```

## Module 0 at a glance {#module-0-overview}

**What you will do.** You will install three free programs: [R](../docs/glossary.md#r) (the language that runs our commands), RStudio (a window that makes R easier to use) and [PLINK 2](../docs/glossary.md#plink-2) (a program that analyses genotype files). You will download the course files and the course data. Then you will run a setup check that shows your computer is ready.

**What you will learn.**

- How to find out which system and processor your computer has.
- How to install R, RStudio and PLINK 2.
- How to open a project and run a command in the console.
- Why checksums and a setup check protect your work.
- The routine you will use in every step: read, run, compare.

**How long it takes.** About 90 minutes. The slowest step is 0.5, because the data archive is large and the R packages must be installed.

## 0.1 What you need {#step-0-1}

### What we do

Prepare a computer, a project folder and the tools used in the whole course. In this step you only find out which system and processor you have.

You can see this without R. On Windows, open Settings, then System, then About, and read "System type". On a Mac, click the Apple menu, then About This Mac. A line "Chip" with a name such as Apple M1 means Apple Silicon. A line "Processor" means an Intel Mac. On Linux, open Settings and look for About or System information. Menu names depend on your distribution.

### Why

R is the language that runs our commands. RStudio gives you a console, a file browser and an editor around R. PLINK 2 is a separate program that processes genotypes. A genotype records the [alleles](../docs/glossary.md#allele) found at one DNA site. An allele is one version of the DNA letter at that site. R starts PLINK for you. Installing R does not install PLINK.

### You need

A Windows, macOS or Linux computer. You need an internet connection to download the software and the approved data. You also need a folder where you can save files. The local data test does not need a network download. Keep free space for three things: the [encrypted archive](../docs/glossary.md#encrypted-archive) (a locked data file that needs a password), an extracted copy of it, and your results. The space you need grows as you work.

### Command

No code to run. Use the system settings described above. Write down your operating system and processor type. You will use them to choose the correct installers.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

You have written down your operating system and processor type. For example, Windows may report a 64-bit system with an x64 processor. A Mac may show Apple Silicon or an Intel processor. The details depend on your computer.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If you cannot find the system information, ask the instructor or your institution's support team. You do not need R for this step.

</details>

### Quick check

Does installing R also install the program that analyses the genotype files?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. PLINK 2 is installed separately at step 0.4.</details>

### Files created

None.

## 0.2 Install R {#step-0-2}

### What we do

Install R from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/), the official website for R. Follow these actions:

1. Open the CRAN page. Click the link for your system: "Download R for Windows", "Download R for macOS" or "Download R for Linux".
2. On Windows, click "base" (or "install R for the first time"). Then click the link at the top that starts with "Download R" and ends with "for Windows".
3. On macOS, click the `.pkg` file for your processor. Use the `arm64` file for Apple Silicon. Use the `x86_64` file for an Intel Mac. File names on the page can change a little.
4. On Linux, follow the CRAN instructions for your distribution. Installing packages may need an administrator.
5. Open the downloaded file. Accept the default choices. Click "Next" on Windows or "Continue" on macOS until the installer ends. If the computer asks for permission or a password, give it.

After the installation you should see a new program called R. On Windows it is in the Start menu. On macOS it is in the Applications folder.

### Why

R reads the commands in the notebooks and runs them. An [R package](../docs/glossary.md#r-package) is an add-on that gives R more functions. Packages do not replace R itself.

### You need

The system and processor you found at step 0.1. On a Mac with Apple Silicon, use the ARM64 build. On an Intel Mac, use the Intel build. Do not mix the two.

### Command

No code to run. Open R from the Start menu or the Applications folder. Check that its window opens. Step 0.7 checks the installed version after you have opened the course project.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The R application opens. Its window shows version information and a `>` prompt. Your version may differ from the Windows validation environment, which used R 4.5.2. The author also tested Ubuntu extraction with R 4.6.1.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If your computer blocks the installation, ask the instructor or your institution's support team for an approved installation. Do not change your system language.

</details>

### Quick check

Does the R installer also install RStudio?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Install RStudio separately at step 0.3.</details>

### Files created

The R installer creates software files outside this course project.

## 0.3 Install RStudio {#step-0-3}

### What we do

Install [RStudio Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) and open it. R must already be installed (step 0.2). Follow these actions:

1. Open the RStudio Desktop page. Click the download button for your operating system. Save the installer file.
2. Open the installer. On Windows, accept the default choices and click "Next" until it ends. On macOS, drag the RStudio icon onto the Applications folder icon in the window that opens. On Linux, follow the instructions on the page.
3. Start RStudio from the Start menu or the Applications folder.

You should see a window with several panes (areas). One pane is called "Console". It shows a `>` prompt.

### Why

The console runs one command at a time. The editor keeps commands in a notebook, so you can read and rerun them later. R holds values, such as loaded data, in memory. These values disappear when R restarts. Files saved on disk remain.

### You need

A working R installation from step 0.2 and the RStudio installer.

### Command

No code to run. Open RStudio from your applications menu. Find the Console pane and check that it shows a `>` prompt. You will run your first course commands at step 0.5.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

RStudio opens and the Console pane shows a `>` prompt. No calculation is required yet.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If RStudio cannot find R, check that you installed R for the correct processor. Restart RStudio after you install R. If the prompt shows `+` instead of `>`, press Escape to return to an empty prompt.

</details>

### Quick check

After restarting R, should you expect an unsaved object to remain in memory?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Reload it from a saved file or rerun the command that creates it.</details>

### Files created

RStudio software files. No course data are created.

## 0.4 Download PLINK 2 {#step-0-4}

### What we do

Get the latest matching build from the [official PLINK 2 page](https://www.cog-genomics.org/plink/2.0/). A build is a version of the program made for one system and processor. Follow these actions:

1. Open the page. It lists several downloads. Choose the build whose name matches your system and processor from step 0.1. The names on the page can change.
2. Save the ZIP file. A ZIP file is one compressed file that holds other files.
3. Extract the ZIP file. On Windows, right-click it, choose "Extract All", then click "Extract". On macOS, double-click it.
4. Inside you find the program. It is `plink2.exe` on Windows and `plink2` on macOS or Linux. This file is the [executable](../docs/glossary.md#executable), the file your computer can run.
5. Copy the executable into the `bin/` folder of the course project. You create the project at step 0.5. The ZIP file may hold other programs too. Copy only `plink2.exe` (or `plink2`).

The ZIP file is not the executable, so extract it first. When you finish, you should see `plink2.exe` or `plink2` inside the `bin` folder.

### Why

PLINK 2 reads the genotype file formats. It computes [quality control](../docs/glossary.md#quality-control) (QC) and association statistics. QC means checks that find samples or data that cannot be trusted. PLINK 1.9 is a different program, so it does not replace PLINK 2. The tested version is stored in one place, the settings file `config.R`. The setup check reports your version and warns you if it differs.

### You need

Your system and processor from step 0.1, and the extracted project from step 0.5. You may download the executable first and copy it after you extract the project.

### Command

No R code to run. Check that you extracted the ZIP and found `plink2.exe` on Windows, or `plink2` on macOS or Linux. Copy it into the project's `bin` folder after step 0.5. The setup check at step 0.7 reports the tested and installed versions.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The extracted executable is named `plink2.exe` on Windows, or `plink2` on macOS or Linux. At step 0.7 your executable must identify itself as PLINK v2. A different build gives a warning. A different version number alone does not make the check fail.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

On macOS or Linux, the extracted file may lack permission to run. Open a terminal in the project folder (the project root). Type `chmod u+x bin/plink2`. This command gives your user permission to run that file. If your institution's security blocks it, ask support. Do not switch off computer security controls.

</details>

### Quick check

Can a file named `plink2.zip` be used as the executable?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Extract the matching executable from it.</details>

### Files created

`bin/plink2.exe` or `bin/plink2`. It stays outside [Git](../docs/glossary.md#git), the tool that records versions of the project files.

## 0.5 Download the course package {#step-0-5}

### What we do

Download and extract the whole source project from its GitHub branch. Then download the matching encrypted data archive from release `data-2026.1`. Follow these actions for the project:

1. Open the GitHub page of the course branch that your instructor gives you. GitHub is a website that stores project files. A branch is one line of versions of a project.
2. Click the green "Code" button. Then click "Download ZIP".
3. Extract the ZIP file into a folder where you can save files, for example in Documents. Use the same method as at step 0.4.
4. Open the extracted folder. You should see the files `config.R` and `GWAS_training_session.Rproj`, and folders such as `R`, `lessons` and `scripts`.

Keep the whole folder together. Do not move single files out of it.

The encrypted data are published in [GitHub Release data-2026.1](https://github.com/mgentiluomo/GWAS_training_session/releases/tag/data-2026.1). The download URLs and SHA-256 checksums are set in `config.R`. The package contains 108 files.

### Why

The source project contains code and text. The encrypted package contains the data. A [checksum](../docs/glossary.md#checksum) is a short code calculated from a file. If the file changes, the code changes. Checksums detect changed or damaged downloads. The password decrypts the archive. A correct password does not replace the checksum check.

### You need

The complete project folder, R and an internet connection. The command below downloads `course-data-2026.1.zip` and its small manifest file, `MANIFEST.tsv`, for you.

Request the password with your university email through the [data access form](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/data-access). In class, you can scan the QR code to open the same form. The form accepts University of Pisa email addresses at `unipi.it` and all its subdomains. Examples include `studenti.unipi.it`, `phd.unipi.it` and `biologia.unipi.it`. It sends the password automatically to these addresses. Other users should write to [manuel.gentiluomo@unipi.it](mailto:manuel.gentiluomo@unipi.it). The password changes every academic year. Do not share it. It never appears in the repository or on the site.

Prepare the packages and helper once in the RStudio console after opening the
project. If you have not opened it yet, do step 0.6 first and return here.

```r
source("R/package_setup.R")
install_course_packages()
source("R/course.R")
```

The first run of `install_course_packages()` can take several minutes. Wait
until the `>` prompt returns.

### Command

Run this command in the RStudio console. It does not run automatically when the
notebook is rendered:

```{r s0-5_data, eval=FALSE}
download_course_data()
```

The function uses `getPass` to ask for a masked password. Type it and press
Enter. You will not see the letters appear. Do not write the password in this
notebook, a shared script or your command history. You do not need 7-Zip.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

On the first successful run, R prints `Course data are ready: 108 files verified.` On a later run with verified data, it prints `Course data are already ready: 108 files verified. Nothing to do.` It does not download or ask for the password again. The data are in the folder `data/course/`. The archive and its small manifest file (a list of the files inside) must both match their configured SHA-256 values. R also checks every extracted data file.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If the download fails, check your internet connection. As a local fallback,
open the release page linked above. Save `course-data-2026.1.zip` and
`MANIFEST.tsv` together in one folder. Then run:

```r
download_course_data(zip_path = file.choose())
```

A file selection window opens. Choose the published ZIP file. Do not choose
the manifest or the project ZIP. The helper checks the same SHA-256 values.

If the data folder exists but cannot be verified, R reports what it found.
This includes a missing manifest, missing files or changed files. For the
standard folder, run the exact recovery command:

```r
download_course_data(overwrite = TRUE)
```

The helper verifies a fresh copy first. It then moves the old folder and its
manifest to a dated backup before replacing them. It prints the backup path.
It never silently deletes the old data. Use that backup if you need earlier work.

Older installations did not keep the verification manifest. They need this
backup and reinstall once. Later runs verify the saved manifest and all data
files without a download or a password prompt.

If R says that the release is not configured, download the current course
project again. If the password is wrong, check your typing and contact the
instructor if needed. Never bypass a checksum failure. See
[troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

If the checksum differs but the password is accepted, should you use that download?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Obtain the approved matching package before continuing.</details>

### Files created

Verified data in `data/course/` and the verification manifest at
`data/course.MANIFEST.tsv`. The manifest stays beside the folder, so the
package still contains 108 files. R removes temporary download and extraction
files. Data, manifests and passwords are never added to Git.

## 0.6 Open the project {#step-0-6}

### What we do

Open the project, then open this notebook. Follow these actions:

1. In the extracted folder, double-click `GWAS_training_session.Rproj`. RStudio opens with the project. You should usually see the project name `GWAS_training_session` at the top right.
2. In the Files pane, click the folder `lessons`. Then click this notebook. It opens in the editor.
3. Run commands in the console. Always work from the [project root](../docs/glossary.md#working-directory), which is the main folder of the project.

### Why

A [relative path](../docs/glossary.md#relative-path) gives the place of a file starting from the working directory. The working directory is the folder where R looks first. One project root means you never copy your personal full paths into commands.

### You need

The complete extracted project from step 0.5, not one downloaded notebook.

### Command

```{r s0-6_project}
getwd()
stopifnot(file.exists("config.R"), file.exists("R/course.R"))
```

Terminal equivalent: from the project directory, run `Rscript -e "stopifnot(file.exists('config.R'))"`. The function `stopifnot` stops with an error when a required condition is false. If the check passes, it prints nothing.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

R prints the path of your project folder. The file checks finish without an error. Your folder path will differ from the author's path.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If `config.R` is missing, close RStudio and open the project again from the extracted source folder. Do not create an empty replacement file. Do not rename a downloaded HTML page to `.R`.

</details>

### Quick check

Does a relative path starting `R/` refer to a folder on every computer's C drive?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. It refers to the R folder under the current project root.</details>

### Files created

RStudio may create local project settings in `.Rproj.user/`. Git ignores them.

## 0.7 Run the setup check {#step-0-7}

### What we do

Run the setup check. It tests the R packages, the [locale](../docs/glossary.md#locale) (your computer's language and number settings), the integrity of the genotype files, and a small PLINK read and write operation. This test uses 20 [variants](../docs/glossary.md#variant), which are DNA positions that differ between people. At the end you should see the message `Preflight passed.`

### Why

A program can print its version and still fail to read data. It can also fail to write results in a folder path that has spaces or non-English letters. A test with a real operation finds these failures before a long analysis.

### You need

The executable from step 0.4 and the verified data from step 0.5. The standard guided data folder is `data/course/`. Some people use an existing external installation. For them, the environment variable `COURSE_DATA_DIR` can name the extracted data, and `COURSE_OUTPUT_DIR` can name a separate output folder. These optional variables contain paths and never passwords.

### Command

```{r s0-7_preflight}
Sys.info()[c("sysname", "release", "machine")]
R.version.string
2 + 3
settings <- new.env(parent = baseenv())
sys.source("config.R", settings)
settings$course_settings$tested_plink_version
source("scripts/preflight.R")
```

Terminal equivalent: `Rscript --vanilla scripts/preflight.R`. The option `--vanilla` starts R without saved workspaces and startup files. Inside the setup check, the R helper runs PLINK with these options. The exact command, with your paths and resource settings, is printed and recorded.

- `--bfile` selects the input files by their shared name prefix. The prefix covers files in the [BED/BIM/FAM](../docs/glossary.md#bed-bim-fam) format.

- `--autosome` keeps only autosomal variants, which are those on chromosomes 1 to 22.

- `--thin-count 20` keeps a small subset of 20 variants, chosen at random.

- `--seed 20261111` sets the starting number of the random choice, so the sampling is repeatable.

- `--freq` reports allele frequencies, which show how common each allele is.

- `--out` sets the prefix of the output files.

For the standard project layout, the plain PLINK command is:

```sh
bin/plink2 --bfile data/course/lab_export/sim2026_lab --autosome --thin-count 20 --seed 20261111 --freq --out results/guided/s0-7_probe --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--threads 2` limits PLINK to two worker threads, which are parts of the computer that work at the same time; `--memory 2048` sets the main workspace of PLINK to 2048 MiB (about 2 gigabytes). On Windows, the executable is `bin\plink2.exe`. The helper also runs a second test on purpose, with a folder name that has non-English letters. It translates that path in a safe way.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

R first prints your system information, its version and the result `[1] 5` from the small calculation. It also prints the tested PLINK version from `config.R`. The guided starting data have 2,016 sample wells and 299,523 variants. A sample well is one position on a laboratory plate that holds one DNA sample. Some wells hold the same person again, which are replicates. The wells represent 2,000 simulated people. PLINK finishes the frequency test on 20 variants. Then R prints `Preflight passed. Report:` followed by the path of the report. The package check may print extra messages. R also prints the PLINK command and PLINK's own messages. One test path shows short names such as `PATHCH~1`. This is normal: it is the safe form of the folder with non-English letters.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Do not run later analysis steps until the setup check succeeds. The setup check explains which package is unavailable or whether the PLINK program is missing. On Windows, the script clears locale requests that R cannot use. This change lasts for the current session only, and your Windows language stays unchanged. Startup warnings can appear before the script has a chance to run. On Linux, the package preparation chooses matching ready-made Posit packages where they exist. If a package must be built from source code, the script explains which development libraries you need.

</details>

### Quick check

Why does the setup check write a frequency report rather than only print a version?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>It tests actual data reading and file writing, including a path containing spaces and non-English characters.</details>

### Files created

`results/guided/software_versions.txt`, `results/guided/preflight.txt` and PLINK test reports in its `path check/` folder. If `COURSE_OUTPUT_DIR` is set, the same files go there instead. No source input is changed.

## 0.8 How to use this guide {#step-0-8}

### What we do

Use the same routine at every step: read, run, compare. Follow these actions:

1. Read "What we do", "Why" and "You need".
2. Run the command in the console.
3. Open "Show the expected result" and compare it with your result.
4. If your result differs, open "If something goes wrong".
5. Answer the quick check.

### Why

If you run all commands at once, the first mistake is hard to find. Saved files give you a way back after a restart. You do not depend on the R workspace, which is lost when R restarts.

### You need

A successful check at step 0.7. Keep the output files and the notebook together in their documented places. The [glossary](../docs/glossary.md) explains the terms used in the course, including quality control, alleles and association.

Every file that the steps create is saved in the folder `results/guided/` of the project. The list "Files created" at the end of each step gives the file names. To look at a file in RStudio, open the Files pane, click `results`, then `guided`.

### Command

Read the list of checkpoints that came with your package. This command changes no files:

```{r s0-8_progress}
source("R/guided.R")
cfg <- guided_init()
where_am_i(data_dir = cfg$data_dir, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

Terminal equivalent: call the R helper through Rscript after you set the same project paths. There is no PLINK command that reports course progress. A [checkpoint](../docs/glossary.md#checkpoint) is a saved state of the course files at the end of a step. The helper `check_step("3.2")` compares step 3.2 with a supplied checkpoint. The helper `restore_checkpoint("3.2")` rebuilds the state after step 3.1, so that you can restart step 3.2. Both protect existing output folders.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Before you start the analysis, every state in the updated checkpoint index is `not verified`. Full genotype sets exist at 2.8, 3.8, 4.6 and 5.7. The other states are rebuilt from stored lists and transformations. Diagnostic and analysis files have their own small checkpoints. The list has about 30 rows, one for each saved state.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

A missing checkpoint does not mean that you failed the analysis. The course package may not supply the baseline, lists or index that the checkpoint needs. Ask for the matching updated package. Do not mix versions. A copied list alone does not recreate the genotypes.

</details>

### Quick check

To restart step 4.2, which completed step's files do you need?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Step 4.1, from the same course data version.</details>

### Files created

`where_am_i` creates no files. Continue to module 1, which explains how the array data arise.

## Module 0 recap {#module-0-recap}

- You found your operating system and processor, and installed R, RStudio and PLINK 2.
- You downloaded the course project and the encrypted data, and checked them with SHA-256 checksums.
- The archive reported `Course data are ready: 108 files verified.`
- The setup check ran PLINK on 20 variants and printed `Preflight passed.`
- The starting data have 2,016 sample wells and 299,523 variants, which represent 2,000 simulated people.
- You learned the routine for every step: read, run, compare.

**Next:** Module 1 explains how the array data arise, from a DNA sample to a scanned chip.
